Click → merge into c1. Total: 1 + 4×2 = 9 actions.

Wait, actually — can the marker skip squares? In level 1, the marker was always the first square cell in that direction (skipping only circles). So movement is one step at a time, and merging happens when a circle is in between.
Hmm, so to merge c2 and c6: bring one next to the other, then merge.

Hmm wait, actually there's a better way: right now the circle at c4 is selected, and the marker is at c2. Instead of merging into c2, what if I aim RIGHT from c4? The marker would be at c5. Select c4, LEFT: the marker is at c2 (skipping c3), click → merge c4+c3 into c2. The circles are at c2, c6. Same as before.
The simplest is: click the current marker (16,20) to merge c4+c3 into c2. Then walk c6 leftward to c3, and merge.
Actually wait — maybe there's a faster way: select c6 first. The default direction for c6 is... the nearest circle is c4 (left). The marker is probably at c5 (the first square to the left of c6). Click → c5. Then select c5: the nearest circle is c4 (left). The marker is at c4?? No — c4 is a circle; the marker skips circles: the first square to the left of c5 = none? c4 is a circle, c3 is a square → the marker is at c3! Click → merge c5+c4 into c3! The circles are at c3, c6. Click → merge into c2. The circles are at c2, c3. Select c3: the marker is at c1 (skipping c2). Click → merge into c1.
Count: 2+2+2+2+2+2 = 12. Worse.
So the plan: click (16,20) [merge into c2], then c6→c5→c4→c3 (6 actions), then select c3 + click c1 (2 actions) = 9 actions total.
